enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (40 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (12 marks); Expression (16 marks); Accuracy (12 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write on from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity (e.g. your name, school, parentage etc). You should write between 450 - 500 words.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Introduction: water as a gift of nature, found everywhere.
2. Description: the forms and appearances of water (dew, streams, lakes, the sea).
3. Uses of water at home, in farming, industry and leisure.
4. Dangers: floods and dirty water.
5. Protection of water and conclusion.

**Model composition (462 words)**

Water is one of the greatest gifts of nature, and no living thing can survive without it. It is colourless, tasteless and odourless, yet it covers about seventy per cent of the surface of the earth and makes up nearly two-thirds of the human body. In my country, Cameroon, water flows in rivers like the Sanaga and the Wouri, falls from the sky in the rainy season, and rises from springs and wells in every village.

Water takes many forms. In the morning, it hangs on the grass as shining drops of dew. At midday, a stream tumbles over the rocks of a waterfall, sparkling like broken glass in the sun. At night, a quiet lake lies still under the moon, so smooth that the stars seem to float on it. When it is very cold, water becomes solid ice, and when it is heated, it rises as steam. The sea, which is salty, roars and rolls against the shore, while the clear water of a village spring whispers softly as it fills a calabash.

The uses of water are countless. At home, we drink it, cook with it, wash our clothes and clean our houses with it. Farmers depend on it to water their crops, and without rain the maize, cassava and cocoa on which many families live would dry up. Factories use it to make drinks, soap and paper, and ships carry goods across it from one country to another. Rivers also provide fish, and dams on them produce electricity that lights our towns. Water also gives joy: children swim in rivers, and families relax on the beaches of Limbe and Kribi during holidays.

However, water can be a danger as well as a blessing. Heavy rains cause floods that destroy houses and farms, and landslides in the hills sometimes bury whole families. Dirty water carries germs that cause cholera, typhoid and diarrhoea, which kill many children every year. In some villages, women and girls walk several kilometres every morning to fetch water, and this wastes time that could be used for study or work.

Because water is so precious, we must protect it. We should not throw rubbish, oil or chemicals into rivers, and we must keep wells and springs clean. We should not waste water by leaving taps running, and we should repair leaking pipes quickly. Planting trees along river banks also protects the sources of streams. Governments should build more boreholes and water systems, especially in rural areas, so that every citizen can have clean drinking water.

In conclusion, water is life. It feeds our bodies, our farms and our industries, and it brings beauty to the world. If we respect it and use it wisely, it will serve us and our children for generations to come.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 12 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 16 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 12 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing only a list of uses of water (a scientific note) without any description or personal voice, so that the composition is flat.
2. Drifting away from the topic, for example by writing a story about a flood, instead of keeping water as the subject.
